t: Section 5136C of the Revised Statutes of the United States (as added by this subtitle) is amended by adding at the end the following:“(h) Clarification of Law Applicable to Nondepository Institution Subsidiaries and Affiliates of National Banks.—“(1) Definitions.—For purposes of this subsection, the terms ‘depository institution’, ‘subsidiary’, and ‘affiliate’ have the same meanings as in section 3 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act.“(2) Rule of construction.—No provision of this title or section 24 of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 371) shall be construed as preempting, annulling, or affecting the applicability of State law to any subsidiary, affiliate, or agent of a national bank (other than a subsidiary, affiliate, or agent that is chartered as a national bank).”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the reference to State law signals federal-state coordination. But this is only a definitions clause and a rule of construction stating that State law is not preempted for nondepository subsidiaries, affiliates, or agents of national banks. It creates no consultation, comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking authority, or right to sue involving any party outside the federal government.
fable.s: shall be construed as preempting, annulling, or affecting the applicability of State law to any subsidiary, affiliate, or agent of a national bank

qwen_block.w: This section is a rule of construction regarding the preemption of state law by federal banking statutes. It does not require the federal government to consult with, coordinate with, or receive input from any outside party (such as states, tribes, or the public) before making a decision. It merely clarifies the legal relationship between federal and state laws.
qwen_block.s: No provision of this title or section 24 of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 371) shall be construed as preempting, annulling, or affecting the applicability of State law to any subsidiary, affiliate, or agent of a national bank

opus.w: This section is only a rule of construction: it says federal banking law does not preempt State law for subsidiaries, affiliates, or agents of national banks that are not themselves national banks. It might look like participation because it mentions "State law," but no State or other outside party is consulted or coordinated with, and no one is given a right to sue over a federal decision. The section also creates no comment period, hearing, rulemaking, or advisory body.
opus.s: No provision of this title or section 24 of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 371) shall be construed as preempting, annulling, or affecting the applicability of State law to any subsidiary, affiliate, or agent of a national bank

qwen_chat.w: This section is a rule of construction that clarifies that federal law does not preempt state law regarding certain subsidiaries of national banks. It does not require the federal government to consult, coordinate with, or seek input from state governments or any other outside parties before making a decision. It simply defines the legal boundary between federal and state jurisdiction without imposing any participatory process.
qwen_chat.s: No provision of this title or section 24 of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 371) shall be construed as preempting, annulling, or affecting the applicability of State law to any subsidiary, affiliate, or agent of a national bank (other than a subsidiary, affiliate, or agent that is chartered as a national bank).
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the section clarifies that State law applies to national bank subsidiaries, it implies a role for state governments in regulating these entities, which could be seen as a form of coordination or participation. However, this is a rule of construction regarding legal preemption, not a procedural requirement for the federal government to consult with or coordinate with state governments before making a decision. The text does not mandate any interaction, consultation, or coordination between federal and state actors; it merely defines the scope of applicable law.
